learn.b: All living things are made of cells. The cell is the basic unit of life. All cells come from other cells. Prokaryotes, like bacteria, have no nucleus. Eukaryotes, like plants and animals, have a nucleus and other membrane-bound organelles.
The nucleus holds the DNA. Ribosomes build proteins. Mitochondria make most of the cell's ATP. The Golgi apparatus packages and ships proteins. Lysosomes digest waste.

learn.h: Plant cells and levels of life
learn.b: Plant cells also have a cell wall, chloroplasts for photosynthesis, and a large central vacuole. Life is organized in levels: cell, tissue, organ, organ system, organism.

qs.q: Which organelle makes most of the cell's ATP?
qs.why: Mitochondria carry out cellular respiration.

qs.q: Which structure is found in plant cells but NOT in animal cells?
qs.why: Plants have a rigid cell wall outside the membrane.

qs.q: Which of these is a prokaryote?
qs.why: Bacteria have no nucleus.

qs.q: Where are proteins built in the cell?
qs.why: Ribosomes read mRNA and join amino acids.

qs.q: Prokaryotic cells have a nucleus.
qs.why: Prokaryotes have no nucleus; their DNA floats in the cytoplasm.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
Put the levels of life in order from smallest to largest

lab.q: Challenge: which organelle is called the 'powerhouse of the cell'?
lab.why: Mitochondria carry out cellular respiration to make ATP.

lab.q: Challenge: a microscope has a 10x eyepiece and a 40x objective lens. What is the total magnification?
Challenge: a cell has no nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles. Is it prokaryotic or eukaryotic?
lab.why: Cells without a nucleus are prokaryotic.

learn.b: Living things are built from four big molecule types. Carbohydrates give quick energy. Lipids store energy and form membranes. Proteins are chains of amino acids and do most of the cell's work. Nucleic acids (DNA and RNA) store information.

Enzymes are proteins that speed up reactions by lowering the activation energy. Each enzyme fits a specific substrate, like a key in a lock. Heat or the wrong pH can change an enzyme's shape so it stops working.

The cell membrane is a phospholipid bilayer. Diffusion moves particles from high to low concentration with no energy needed. Osmosis is the diffusion of water across a membrane. Active transport moves particles against the gradient and uses energy (ATP).

qs.q: What are the building blocks (monomers) of proteins?
qs.why: Proteins are chains of amino acids.

qs.q: What does an enzyme do?
o: Lowers the activation energy of a reaction
qs.why: Enzymes are biological catalysts.

qs.q: What is osmosis?
o: Movement of water across a membrane
Movement of proteins into the nucleus
qs.why: Osmosis is the diffusion of water.

qs.q: What makes active transport different from diffusion?
o: It moves particles from high to low concentration
It uses energy to move particles against a gradient
qs.why: Active transport uses ATP to go against the gradient.

qs.q: Diffusion requires the cell to use ATP.
qs.why: Diffusion is passive, so it needs no cell energy.

qs.q: Match each molecule type to its role
Order from smallest to largest

lab.q: Challenge: what type of molecule is an enzyme?
Challenge: what is the monomer (building block) of a nucleic acid called?
lab.hint: DNA and RNA are chains of these.
lab.why: Nucleic acids are chains of nucleotides.

lab.q: Challenge: a cell is placed in pure water. Water moves in by osmosis. Does the cell swell or shrink?
lab.hint: Water moves to where there is more solute.
lab.why: The cell has more solute than pure water, so water enters and it swells.

learn.b: Photosynthesis has two stages. The light reactions happen in the thylakoid membranes and capture light energy. The Calvin cycle happens in the stroma and uses that energy to build sugar from carbon dioxide.

Glycolysis splits glucose in the cytoplasm and does not need oxygen. The Krebs cycle and the electron transport chain happen in the mitochondria and need oxygen. Together they make about 36 to 38 ATP per glucose.
Mitosis makes two identical body cells. Its phases are prophase, metaphase, anaphase, and telophase. Meiosis makes four different gametes, each with half the number of chromosomes (haploid).

qs.q: Where do the light reactions of photosynthesis occur?
qs.why: Thylakoids hold the chlorophyll.

qs.q: Which stage of cellular respiration happens in the cytoplasm and needs no oxygen?
qs.why: Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm.

qs.q: What does mitosis produce?
qs.why: Mitosis makes identical daughter cells.

qs.q: What does meiosis produce?
qs.why: Meiosis halves the chromosome number to make gametes.

qs.q: Chromosomes line up in the middle of the cell during anaphase.
qs.why: They line up during metaphase; in anaphase the sister chromatids separate.

qs.q: Match each process to its description
Put the phases of mitosis in order

lab.q: Challenge: what sugar is made by photosynthesis?
Challenge: a body cell with 46 chromosomes divides by mitosis. How many chromosomes are in each new cell?
lab.why: Mitosis keeps the chromosome number the same.

lab.q: Challenge: a human cell with 46 chromosomes goes through meiosis. How many chromosomes are in each gamete?

learn.b: DNA is a double helix made of nucleotides. The bases pair in a fixed way: A with T, and C with G. In replication, each strand is used as a template to build a new matching strand.

In transcription, DNA is copied into mRNA in the nucleus. In translation, a ribosome reads the mRNA three bases (a codon) at a time and joins amino acids into a protein. RNA uses uracil (U) instead of thymine.
Mendel showed that each parent gives one allele for a gene. A genotype is the alleles, such as AA, Aa, or aa. Heterozygous means two different alleles. A mutation is a change in the DNA sequence.

qs.q: In DNA, which base pairs with adenine (A)?
qs.why: A pairs with T in DNA.

qs.q: What is made during transcription?
qs.why: DNA is copied into messenger RNA.

qs.q: Where does translation take place?
qs.why: Ribosomes build proteins from mRNA.

qs.q: Which genotype is heterozygous?
qs.why: Heterozygous means two different alleles.

qs.q: In RNA, adenine pairs with thymine.
qs.why: RNA has uracil instead of thymine.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
pairs: Three bases that code for an amino acid
Copy of a gene sent out of nucleus

qs.q: Order the steps from gene to protein

lab.q: Challenge: a DNA strand reads ATTGC. Write the complementary strand.
lab.hint: A pairs with T, C pairs with G.
lab.why: A-T, T-A, T-A, G-C, C-G gives TAACG.

lab.q: Challenge: in a cross of Aa x Aa, what fraction of offspring are aa?
lab.why: The cross gives AA, Aa, Aa, aa, so 1 in 4 is aa.

lab.q: Challenge: an mRNA has 12 bases and no stop codon. How many amino acids does it code for?

learn.b: A mutation is a change in the DNA sequence. A substitution swaps one base. An insertion or deletion adds or removes bases and can cause a frameshift, which changes every codon after it. All your cells have the same DNA, but each cell type turns on different genes.

PCR makes millions of copies of a DNA segment using heat cycles and DNA polymerase. Gel electrophoresis separates DNA fragments by size. DNA is negative, so it moves toward the positive end, and the smallest pieces travel farthest.

CRISPR can cut DNA at a chosen spot to edit a gene. Scientists can also put a human gene, like the one for insulin, into a bacterial plasmid so bacteria make the protein. An organism with added genes is called transgenic or a GMO.

qs.q: What does PCR do?
o: Makes many copies of a DNA segment
qs.why: PCR amplifies a chosen DNA segment.

qs.q: In gel electrophoresis, which DNA fragments travel the farthest?
o: The fragments with the most A bases
qs.why: Small pieces move through the gel more easily.

qs.q: Deleting one base from the middle of a gene usually causes what?
o: A change in only one amino acid
qs.why: The reading frame shifts, changing all later codons.

qs.q: Why do muscle cells and nerve cells look different if they have the same DNA?
o: They have different numbers of genes
qs.why: Gene expression differs between cell types.

qs.q: In gel electrophoresis, DNA fragments move toward the positive electrode.
qs.why: DNA has a negative charge, so it is pulled toward the positive end.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
Put the steps of one PCR cycle in order
items: The cycle repeats to double the copies

lab.q: Challenge: a DNA template strand reads TAC GGA. Write the mRNA (no spaces).
lab.hint: A pairs with U in RNA.
lab.why: TAC pairs to AUG, and GGA pairs to CCU.

lab.q: Challenge: PCR doubles the DNA every cycle. Starting from 1 molecule, how many copies after 5 cycles?
Challenge: which enzyme builds the new DNA strands in PCR? (two words)
lab.why: DNA polymerase adds nucleotides to the primers.

learn.b: Natural selection acts on variation in a population. Homologous structures, like the limb bones of humans, whales, and bats, show common ancestry. New species often form when populations become separated and stop interbreeding.

Energy enters from the Sun and is captured by producers. Only about 10 percent of energy passes from one trophic level to the next. The rest is lost as heat. Energy flows one way, while matter like carbon and nitrogen is recycled.
Populations can grow quickly at first. Carrying capacity is the largest population an environment can support with its food, water, and space.

qs.q: About what percent of energy passes to the next trophic level?
qs.why: About 90 percent is lost, mostly as heat.

qs.q: What is carrying capacity?
o: The largest population an environment can support
The number of species in an area
qs.why: Resources set the limit.

qs.q: What often starts the formation of a new species?
qs.why: Separated groups can no longer interbreed and diverge.

qs.q: What do homologous structures suggest?
qs.why: Similar bone patterns point to a shared ancestor.

qs.q: In ecosystems, energy is recycled while matter flows in one direction.
qs.why: It is the opposite: energy flows one way and matter is recycled.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
pairs: Similar structures from a common ancestor

qs.q: Order the trophic levels, starting with the producer

lab.q: Challenge: grass has 10000 J of energy. How many joules reach the frog in grass -> grasshopper -> frog? (10% rule)
Challenge: what is the largest population an environment can support called? (two words)
lab.why: Food, water, and space set the carrying capacity.

lab.q: Challenge: structures like the human arm and whale flipper share a similar bone layout. What word describes them?
lab.why: Homologous structures come from a shared ancestor.

learn.b: Homeostasis is keeping the body's inside conditions steady. Most control uses negative feedback, which reverses a change. When you get too hot, you sweat, and the sweat cools you back toward normal, about 37 degrees Celsius.

The circulatory system uses the heart, blood vessels, and blood to carry oxygen and nutrients. Arteries carry blood away from the heart. In the lungs, oxygen enters the blood through tiny air sacs called alveoli, and carbon dioxide leaves.

In digestion, enzymes break food down and the small intestine absorbs most nutrients. The nervous system sends fast electrical signals through neurons. The endocrine system uses hormones: the pancreas releases insulin to lower blood sugar. The kidneys filter the blood.

qs.q: Where does gas exchange happen in the lungs?
qs.why: Alveoli are thin air sacs surrounded by capillaries.

qs.q: Which hormone lowers blood glucose?
qs.why: The pancreas releases insulin when blood sugar is high.

qs.q: Where is most nutrient absorption done?
qs.why: The small intestine has a huge surface area for absorption.

qs.q: What does negative feedback do?
o: Reverses a change to return to a set point
qs.why: It keeps conditions such as temperature stable.

qs.q: Arteries carry blood away from the heart.
qs.why: Arteries move blood away; veins return it.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
Put the path of blood in order, starting at the right side of the heart

lab.q: Challenge: what is normal human body temperature in degrees Celsius?
lab.why: Normal body temperature is about 37 C.

lab.q: Challenge: which hormone does the pancreas release when blood sugar is high?
lab.why: Insulin helps cells take up glucose.

lab.q: Challenge: a heart beats 70 times per minute. How many beats in 10 minutes?

learn.b: Bacteria are living prokaryotic cells that reproduce by binary fission. Viruses are not cells. A virus is genetic material inside a protein coat, and it can only reproduce inside a host cell. Antibiotics kill bacteria but do not work on viruses.

A pathogen is a germ that causes disease. Skin and mucus are the first barrier. White blood cells then attack. An antigen is a marker on a pathogen. B cells make antibodies, proteins that bind to a specific antigen.

A vaccine shows the immune system a harmless piece or weak form of a germ. The body makes antibodies and memory cells. If the real germ comes later, the memory cells respond fast, so you often do not get sick.

qs.q: Antibiotics are used to treat infections caused by what?
qs.why: Antibiotics target bacterial cells, not viruses.

qs.q: How do bacteria reproduce?
qs.why: One cell splits into two identical cells.

qs.q: What does a vaccine do?
o: Kills all bacteria in the body
Trains the immune system to recognize a germ
Makes the body stop making antibodies
qs.why: It builds memory cells without causing the disease.

qs.q: Which cells make antibodies?
qs.why: B cells are a type of white blood cell that produce antibodies.

qs.q: Viruses are made of cells.
qs.why: Viruses are not cells; they need a host cell to reproduce.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
Put the steps of a virus infecting a cell in order
items: Virus attaches to a host cell
Virus puts its genetic material inside

lab.q: Challenge: a bacterium divides every 20 minutes. Starting from 1 cell, how many cells after 2 hours?
Challenge: what word means a disease-causing organism?
lab.why: A pathogen is a germ that causes disease.

lab.q: Challenge: which blood cells fight infection? (three words)
lab.why: White blood cells make up the immune response.

learn.b: Matter is anything with mass that takes up space. In a solid, particles are packed and vibrate. In a liquid they slide past each other. In a gas they are far apart and move freely. Melting, freezing, boiling, and condensing are changes of state.

In a physical change, no new substance forms. Melting ice and dissolving salt are examples. In a chemical change, new substances form. Rusting, burning, and cooking an egg are examples. Signs include gas bubbles, a color change, or heat and light.

An element has one kind of atom. A compound has two or more elements bonded together. A mixture is not chemically joined. Density is mass divided by volume: D = m / V. A 20 g sample with a volume of 5 cm^3 has a density of 4 g/cm^3.

qs.q: Which of these is a chemical change?
qs.why: Rust is a new substance, iron oxide.

qs.q: What is the change from gas to liquid called?
qs.why: Gas particles slow down and join into a liquid.

qs.q: A sample has a mass of 20 g and a volume of 5 cm^3. What is its density?
Salt fully dissolved in water is an example of what?
qs.why: It looks the same throughout and can be separated by evaporation.

qs.q: Melting is a chemical change.
qs.why: Melting only changes the state; no new substance forms.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
Put the changes in order as ice is heated

lab.q: Challenge: a block has a mass of 60 g and a volume of 12 cm^3. What is its density in g/cm^3?
Challenge: what is the change from a solid directly to a gas called?
Challenge: a liquid has a density of 2.5 g/mL. What is the mass of 8 mL in grams?

learn.b: An atom has protons and neutrons in the nucleus and electrons outside it. The atomic number is the number of protons. Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons.
Electrons sit in energy levels. The outer-shell electrons are called valence electrons. For main-group elements, the group number tells how many: group 1 has 1, and group 17 has 7.
Atomic radius increases going down a group. Alkali metals (group 1) are very reactive. Halogens (group 17) are reactive nonmetals. Noble gases (group 18) are stable and rarely react.

qs.q: What do isotopes of an element have in common?
qs.why: Isotopes differ only in neutrons.

qs.q: How many valence electrons does a halogen (group 17) atom have?
qs.why: Group 17 elements have 7 valence electrons.

qs.q: How does atomic radius change going down a group?
qs.why: More energy levels make the atom larger.

qs.q: Which group contains the very reactive metals like sodium and potassium?
qs.why: Alkali metals are group 1.

qs.q: The atomic number of an element equals its number of neutrons.
qs.why: The atomic number equals the number of protons.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
Order by increasing atomic number

lab.q: Challenge: an atom has atomic number 17 and mass number 35. How many neutrons does it have?
Challenge: a neutral atom has 8 protons. How many electrons does it have?
lab.why: Electrons equal protons in a neutral atom.

lab.q: Challenge: what family of elements is group 18? (two words)

learn.b: In an ionic bond, one atom transfers electrons to another, making positive and negative ions that attract each other. It usually forms between a metal and a nonmetal, like sodium chloride (NaCl).
In a covalent bond, atoms share electrons. It usually forms between nonmetals, like in H2O and CO2. A molecule is a group of atoms joined by covalent bonds.
If one atom pulls shared electrons harder, the bond is polar. Oxygen pulls harder than hydrogen, so water is a polar molecule. Cations are positive ions and anions are negative ions.

qs.q: What kind of bond holds sodium and chlorine together in NaCl?
qs.why: Sodium gives an electron to chlorine.

qs.q: What happens in a covalent bond?
qs.why: Covalent bonds are shared pairs of electrons.

qs.q: Which pair of elements is most likely to form an ionic compound?
qs.why: A metal and a nonmetal usually bond ionically.

qs.q: Why is water a polar molecule?
o: Oxygen pulls the shared electrons harder
qs.why: Unequal sharing creates partial charges.

qs.q: Ionic compounds are made of molecules that share electrons.
qs.why: Ionic compounds are lattices of ions attracted by opposite charges.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
Order the steps of forming NaCl

lab.q: Challenge: what type of bond forms between sodium and chlorine in NaCl?
lab.why: Sodium transfers an electron to chlorine.

lab.q: Challenge: what type of bond shares electrons between two nonmetals?
lab.why: Nonmetals share electrons in covalent bonds.

lab.q: Challenge: a magnesium atom loses 2 electrons. What is the charge of the ion? (like 1+)
lab.hint: Losing negative charge makes it positive.
lab.why: It has two more protons than electrons, so the charge is 2+.

learn.b: A mole is 6.02 x 10^23 particles (Avogadro's number). Molar mass is the mass of one mole in grams. For water (H2O) it is 2(1) + 16 = 18 g/mol.
Atoms are conserved, so a balanced equation has the same number of each atom on both sides. Coefficients are changed, not subscripts. For example, 2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O is balanced.

Synthesis: two or more reactants make one product. Decomposition: one reactant breaks into simpler ones. Combustion: a fuel burns with oxygen. Single and double replacement swap parts between compounds.

qs.q: What is Avogadro's number?
qs.why: One mole contains 6.02 x 10^23 particles.

qs.q: What is the molar mass of water (H2O)?
In 2H2 + O2 -> ?H2O, what coefficient balances the water?
qs.why: Four H atoms and two O atoms make 2 H2O.

qs.q: What type of reaction is 2H2O -> 2H2 + O2?
qs.why: One compound breaks into simpler substances.

qs.q: The number of atoms of each element changes in a balanced equation.
qs.why: Atoms are conserved, so each element has equal atoms on both sides.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
Order the steps to convert grams to particles

lab.q: Challenge: what is the molar mass of CO2 in g/mol? (C = 12, O = 16)
Challenge: how many moles are in 88 g of CO2?
Challenge: what is the mass of 3 moles of H2O in grams? (18 g/mol)

learn.b: Molarity (M) is moles of solute per liter of solution. If you dissolve 2 moles of NaCl to make 4 L of solution, the molarity is 2/4 = 0.5 M.

Boyle's law: at constant temperature, if the volume of a gas decreases, its pressure increases. Charles's law: at constant pressure, volume increases as temperature increases. Gas laws need temperature in kelvins (K = C + 273).
Acids donate H+ ions, and bases accept H+ or release OH-. A pH below 7 is acidic, 7 is neutral, and above 7 is basic. Neutralization: acid + base -> salt + water.

qs.q: What is molarity?
o: Moles of solute per liter of solution
qs.why: M = moles / liters.

qs.q: What is the molarity of 2 moles of NaCl dissolved to make 4 L of solution?
qs.why: 2 moles / 4 L = 0.5 M.

qs.q: At constant temperature, what happens to the pressure of a gas if its volume decreases?
qs.why: This is Boyle's law.

qs.q: Which pH value is basic?
qs.why: A pH above 7 is basic.

qs.q: Gas law calculations should use temperature in degrees Celsius.
qs.why: They must use kelvins.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
pairs: Acid + base makes salt and water

qs.q: Order from coldest to hottest

lab.q: Challenge: 3 moles of solute are dissolved to make 1.5 L of solution. What is the molarity (M)?
Challenge: a gas at 1 atm in 2 L is squeezed to 0.5 L at constant temperature. What is the new pressure in atm?
lab.why: 1 x 2 = P2 x 0.5, so P2 = 4 atm.

lab.q: Challenge: a solution has [H+] = 0.001 M (1 x 10^-3). What is its pH?

learn.b: An exothermic reaction releases energy to the surroundings, so the temperature rises. An endothermic reaction absorbs energy, so things feel cold. Activation energy is the energy needed to start a reaction.

Collision theory says particles must collide with enough energy and the right orientation. Rates go up with higher temperature, higher concentration, and more surface area (like a powder). A catalyst speeds up a reaction by lowering the activation energy and is not used up.

In a reversible reaction, the forward and reverse rates become equal at equilibrium, so amounts stay constant. Le Chatelier's principle says a system shifts to oppose a change. Adding more reactant shifts the reaction toward the products.

qs.q: In an exothermic reaction, what happens to energy?
o: It is released to the surroundings
It is absorbed from the surroundings
It stays exactly the same everywhere
qs.why: Exothermic reactions give off heat.

qs.q: Which change would speed up a reaction of a solid?
qs.why: More surface area means more collisions.

qs.q: What is true at equilibrium?
o: Forward and reverse rates are equal
qs.why: Both reactions continue at the same rate.

qs.q: Adding more reactant to a system at equilibrium shifts it toward what?
qs.why: The system shifts to use up the added reactant.

qs.q: A catalyst is used up during the reaction.
qs.why: A catalyst is regenerated and is not consumed.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
pairs: Speeds up without being used up

qs.q: Put the steps of a successful collision in order
items: The collision has enough energy and the right angle

lab.q: Challenge: how much heat (in J) warms 100 g of water by 10 C? (c = 4.18 J/g C)
Challenge: suppose a reaction rate doubles for every 10 C rise. The rate is 3 units at 20 C. What is it at 40 C?
Challenge: what principle predicts how an equilibrium shifts when you change conditions?
lab.why: Le Chatelier's principle: the system shifts to oppose the change.

learn.b: Oxidation is the loss of electrons. Reduction is the gain of electrons. Remember OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain. They always happen together. In Zn + Cu2+ -> Zn2+ + Cu, zinc is oxidized and copper ions are reduced.

An oxidation number is the charge an atom would have if electrons were fully transferred. A pure element is 0. Na in NaCl is +1 and Cl is -1. Oxygen is usually -2. If the number goes up, the atom was oxidized.

A battery is a galvanic cell: a spontaneous redox reaction makes electric current. Oxidation happens at the anode and reduction at the cathode. Electrolysis uses electricity to force a reaction. Rusting is the slow oxidation of iron.

qs.q: What does oxidation mean?
qs.why: OIL: Oxidation Is Loss.

qs.q: In Zn + Cu2+ -> Zn2+ + Cu, which species is oxidized?
qs.why: Zinc loses two electrons.

qs.q: What is the oxidation number of oxygen in most compounds?
qs.why: Oxygen is usually -2, except in peroxides.

qs.q: In a battery (galvanic cell), chemical energy is converted into what?
qs.why: The redox reaction pushes electrons through a wire.

qs.q: Reduction is the loss of electrons.
qs.why: Reduction is the gain of electrons.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
Put the steps in a zinc-copper cell in order
items: Copper ions gain electrons and plate out

lab.q: Challenge: what is the oxidation number of Na in NaCl?
lab.why: Na+ has an oxidation number of +1.

lab.q: Challenge: what is the oxidation number of Cl in NaCl?
lab.why: Cl- has an oxidation number of -1.

lab.q: Challenge: in Mg + 2HCl -> MgCl2 + H2, which element is oxidized? (name or symbol)
lab.why: Mg goes from 0 to +2, so it is oxidized.

learn.b: Unstable nuclei decay. An alpha particle is a helium nucleus (2 protons, 2 neutrons). A beta particle is a fast electron. Gamma rays are high-energy waves. A half-life is the time for half of a sample to decay: 80 g becomes 40 g, then 20 g.

Fission splits a heavy nucleus, like uranium, into smaller ones and is used in nuclear power plants. Fusion joins light nuclei, like hydrogen, into heavier ones and powers the Sun. Both release huge amounts of energy.

Organic chemistry is the chemistry of carbon compounds. Carbon forms four bonds. Alkanes have only single bonds: methane CH4, ethane C2H6, propane C3H8, butane C4H10. Alkenes have a C=C double bond. An alcohol has an -OH group.

qs.q: A sample has a half-life of 10 days. How much of an 80 g sample is left after 20 days?
qs.why: Two half-lives: 80 -> 40 -> 20.

qs.q: What is an alpha particle?
qs.why: It has 2 protons and 2 neutrons.

qs.q: How many bonds does each carbon atom usually form?
qs.why: Carbon has 4 valence electrons.

qs.q: Which of these is an alkane?
qs.why: Alkanes follow CnH(2n+2): C3H8 fits.

qs.q: Fusion splits a heavy nucleus into smaller ones.
qs.why: That is fission; fusion joins light nuclei.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
pairs: Joins light nuclei, like in the Sun

qs.q: Put the alkanes in order by number of carbons, fewest first

lab.q: Challenge: a 64 g sample has a half-life of 5 years. How many grams remain after 15 years?
Challenge: how many carbon atoms are in a molecule of propane?
Challenge: what is the name of the alkane with 1 carbon?

learn.b: Displacement is the change in position, with direction. Velocity is speed with direction: v = d / t. Acceleration is how fast velocity changes: a = (change in v) / t.
For an object starting from rest with constant acceleration, v = at and d = (1/2)at^2. An object moving at constant velocity has zero acceleration.
Near Earth, objects in free fall accelerate downward at about 9.8 m/s^2 (g). Every second, the falling speed grows by about 9.8 m/s.

qs.q: A car speeds up from 0 to 20 m/s in 4 s. What is its acceleration?
What is the acceleration due to gravity near Earth's surface?
qs.why: g is about 9.8 m/s^2.

qs.q: What is the acceleration of an object moving at constant velocity?
qs.why: No change in velocity means zero acceleration.

qs.q: An object starts from rest and accelerates at 2 m/s^2 for 5 s. How far does it travel?
Speed and velocity mean exactly the same thing.
qs.why: Velocity includes direction; speed does not.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
Order a dropped object's speed from earliest to latest

lab.q: Challenge: a runner covers 150 m in 10 s at constant speed. What is the speed in m/s?
Challenge: a car goes from 0 to 20 m/s in 4 s. What is its acceleration in m/s^2?
Challenge: a ball falls from rest for 3 s. What is its speed in m/s? (g = 9.8)

learn.b: The net force is the sum of all forces on an object, with direction. A 10 N force to the right and a 4 N force to the left give a net force of 6 N to the right.
Net force equals mass times acceleration: F = ma. A bigger force gives more acceleration, and a bigger mass gives less. Weight is the force of gravity on a mass: W = mg.

The normal force is the push of a surface perpendicular to it. Friction opposes sliding. In a vacuum, heavy and light objects fall at the same rate because gravity gives all masses the same acceleration.

qs.q: A 3 kg object has a net force of 15 N. What is its acceleration?
What is the weight of a 10 kg object? (Use g = 9.8 m/s^2.)
A 10 N force pushes right and a 4 N force pushes left. What is the net force?
qs.why: 10 - 4 = 6 N to the right.

qs.q: What is the normal force?
o: Support force perpendicular to a surface
qs.why: A surface pushes back at 90 degrees to itself.

qs.q: In a vacuum, a heavier object always falls faster than a lighter one.
qs.why: All objects fall with the same acceleration in a vacuum.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
pairs: Force of gravity on a mass

qs.q: Order the acceleration of a 2 kg object, smallest first

lab.q: Challenge: a 5 kg cart accelerates at 3 m/s^2. What is the net force in N?
Challenge: forces of 20 N right and 8 N left act on a box. What is the net force in N?
Challenge: what is the weight in N of a 60 kg person? (g = 9.8)

learn.b: An object moving in a circle changes direction all the time, so it accelerates even at constant speed. The centripetal force points toward the center of the circle. The acceleration is a = v^2 / r. A 6 m/s object on a 3 m circle has a = 36 / 3 = 12 m/s^2.

Every two masses attract each other. The force grows with the masses and gets weaker with distance: if the distance doubles, the force becomes one fourth, and if it triples, one ninth. Mass is the amount of matter and never changes. Weight is the gravity force, W = mg.

A satellite in orbit is in continuous free fall. It keeps falling toward the planet but moves sideways fast enough to keep missing it. That is why astronauts seem weightless. On the Moon, g is about 1.6 m/s^2, so weight is smaller but mass is the same.

qs.q: In which direction does the centripetal force point?
o: Toward the center of the circle
qs.why: It pulls the object inward, keeping it on the circle.

qs.q: If the distance between two masses doubles, the gravitational force becomes what?
qs.why: Gravity follows an inverse-square law.

qs.q: On the Moon g is about 1.6 m/s^2. What is the weight of a 10 kg mass there?
Why do astronauts float inside the space station?
o: The station is outside the atmosphere's weight
They are in continuous free fall
qs.why: Gravity is still strong; they and the station fall together.

qs.why: Mass stays the same; only the weight changes.

Force of gravity on a mass

learn.b: Work equals force times distance: W = Fd, measured in joules (J). Power is work per time: P = W / t, measured in watts (W). Pushing with 10 N over 5 m does 50 J of work.
Kinetic energy is KE = (1/2)mv^2. Gravitational potential energy is PE = mgh. Energy is conserved. When friction slows an object, its kinetic energy becomes thermal energy, not nothing.
Momentum is p = mv, measured in kg m/s. In a collision with no outside forces, the total momentum before equals the total momentum after.

What is the momentum of a 2 kg object moving at 3 m/s?
What is the SI unit of power?
qs.why: Power is measured in watts.

qs.q: What is the kinetic energy of a 2 kg object moving at 3 m/s?
Energy is destroyed when friction slows an object down.
qs.why: The kinetic energy becomes thermal energy.

Three quarters of the way down

learn.b: Temperature measures the average kinetic energy of particles. Heat is thermal energy moving from a hotter object to a colder one. The Kelvin scale starts at absolute zero: K = C + 273. The heat needed to warm a material is Q = mc(change in T), where c is the specific heat.

Conduction moves heat through direct contact, like a spoon heating in soup. Convection moves heat in a flowing fluid, like warm air rising. Radiation moves heat as electromagnetic waves and needs no matter, like sunlight crossing space.

The first law says energy is conserved: heat added can raise thermal energy or do work. The second law says heat flows on its own only from hot to cold, and disorder (entropy) tends to increase. No engine can turn all heat into work.

qs.q: How does the Sun's energy reach Earth?
qs.why: Radiation can cross empty space.

qs.q: In which direction does heat flow by itself?
o: From low mass to high mass
qs.why: That is the second law of thermodynamics.

qs.q: How much heat warms 2 kg of water by 5 C? (c = 4200 J/kg C)
Which is an example of conduction?
o: Warm air rising from a heater
A metal spoon heating up in hot soup
qs.why: Heat passes through direct contact.

qs.q: Temperature measures the total thermal energy of an object.
qs.why: Temperature is the average kinetic energy of particles, not the total.

learn.b: Wave speed equals frequency times wavelength: v = f x wavelength. A wave with a frequency of 10 Hz and a wavelength of 3 m travels at 30 m/s.
Voltage is the energy per charge, current is the flow of charge, and resistance opposes the current. Ohm's law is V = IR. Voltage is in volts, current in amps (A), and resistance in ohms.

In a series circuit, there is one path, so the same current flows through every part, and if one bulb breaks, all go out. In a parallel circuit, there are several paths, and each branch has the same voltage.

qs.q: A wave has a frequency of 10 Hz and a wavelength of 3 m. What is its speed?
qs.why: v = f x wavelength = 10 x 3.

qs.q: A 12 V battery is connected across a 4 ohm resistor. What is the current?
What is the unit of electrical resistance?
qs.why: Resistance is measured in ohms.

qs.q: In a series circuit, what happens if one bulb burns out?
o: The others get dimmer but stay on
qs.why: A series circuit has only one path for current.

qs.q: In a series circuit, the current has several separate paths to take.
qs.why: Several paths describe a parallel circuit.

Order the current from smallest to largest when 12 V is across each resistor

learn.b: Protons are positive and electrons are negative. Like charges repel and opposite charges attract. Rubbing materials together can move electrons and make static electricity. Electric power is P = IV, and energy is E = Pt.

Every magnet has a north and a south pole. Like poles repel and opposite poles attract. A moving charge or current makes a magnetic field. A coil of wire with current is an electromagnet, which can be switched on and off.

Moving a magnet near a coil of wire pushes charges through it. This is electromagnetic induction, and it is how generators work. Transformers change the voltage of alternating current. Power plants use heat to make steam that turns a turbine connected to a generator.

qs.q: What happens between two negative charges?
qs.why: Like charges repel.

qs.q: A device runs at 12 V and 2 A. What is its power?
What happens in a generator?
o: A magnet moves near a coil and makes current
qs.why: That is electromagnetic induction.

qs.q: What do two north poles of magnets do when brought together?
qs.why: Like poles repel.

qs.q: An electric current in a wire creates a magnetic field.
qs.why: Moving charges make magnetic fields, which is how electromagnets work.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
pairs: Magnet made by current in a coil

qs.q: Put the steps in a power plant in order

learn.b: Light is an electromagnetic wave. It travels at 3 x 10^8 m/s in a vacuum and needs no medium. The spectrum from lowest to highest frequency is radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma. Remember c = f x wavelength.

In reflection, light bounces off a surface, and the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. In refraction, light bends when it goes from one material into another because its speed changes. A convex lens bends light rays together (converges). A concave lens spreads them out.

Light also acts like tiny packets of energy called photons. Higher-frequency light has more energy per photon, so gamma rays are more energetic than radio waves. Atoms have a tiny dense nucleus with electrons around it, and electrons give off light when they drop to lower energy levels.

qs.q: Which travels fastest in a vacuum?
qs.why: Light travels at 3 x 10^8 m/s.

qs.q: What does the law of reflection say?
o: The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection
The reflected angle is double the incoming angle
qs.why: The two angles are equal.

qs.q: What does a convex lens do to parallel light rays?
qs.why: A convex lens converges light.

qs.q: Which type of electromagnetic wave has the highest frequency here?
qs.why: Gamma rays are at the top of the spectrum.

qs.q: Light needs a medium, like air, to travel.
qs.why: Light travels through empty space, as sunlight does.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
Put these in order of increasing frequency

lab.q: Challenge: a light ray hits a mirror with an angle of incidence of 35 degrees. What is the angle of reflection in degrees?
Challenge: a light wave has f = 1 x 10^8 Hz and speed 3 x 10^8 m/s. What is its wavelength in m?

learn.b: Earth has four main spheres: the atmosphere (air), hydrosphere (water), lithosphere (rock and soil), and biosphere (life). The air is about 78 percent nitrogen and 21 percent oxygen. Weather happens in the lowest layer, the troposphere. The ozone layer is in the stratosphere above it.

In the water cycle, water evaporates, condenses into clouds, falls as precipitation, and runs off or soaks in. Plants also release water vapor, called transpiration. In the carbon cycle, photosynthesis takes CO2 out of the air, while respiration, decay, and burning fuels put it back.

Plants need nitrogen, but they cannot use nitrogen gas from the air. Nitrogen-fixing bacteria turn it into ammonia that plants can take up. Soil forms in layers: topsoil is rich in organic matter, subsoil is below it, and bedrock is at the bottom.

qs.q: In which atmospheric layer does most weather happen?
qs.why: The troposphere is the lowest layer and holds most of the air.

qs.q: Which process removes CO2 from the air?
qs.why: Plants use CO2 to make sugar.

qs.q: What do nitrogen-fixing bacteria do?
o: Turn nitrogen gas into forms plants can use
qs.why: They convert N2 into ammonia.

qs.q: Which sphere includes oceans, lakes, and ice?
qs.why: Hydro means water.

qs.q: Most of Earth's atmosphere is oxygen.
qs.why: About 78 percent is nitrogen.

Challenge: in which atmospheric layer is the ozone layer found?
lab.why: The ozone layer is in the stratosphere.

lab.why: Plants lose water vapor through their leaves by transpiration.

learn.b: Biotic factors are living parts, like plants and animals. Abiotic factors are nonliving parts, like sunlight, water, and temperature. Biodiversity is the variety of life in an area.

A keystone species has a large effect on its ecosystem compared to how many there are. Losing it can change the whole system. Invasive species are non-native species that spread and harm native species by outcompeting them.
Succession is the slow change in a community over time. Primary succession starts on bare rock: lichens and moss come first, then grasses and shrubs, then forest.

qs.q: Which of these is an abiotic factor?
qs.why: Sunlight is nonliving.

qs.q: What is a keystone species?
o: A species with a very large effect on its ecosystem
A species that only eats plants
qs.why: Its removal changes the whole ecosystem.

qs.q: Why can invasive species be harmful?
qs.why: They use up resources native species need.

qs.q: What is biodiversity?
o: The number of people in an area
The variety of life in an area
qs.why: Biodiversity means variety of species and life.

qs.q: Losing a keystone species usually has little effect on an ecosystem.
qs.why: Keystone species have a very large effect, so losing one can cause major changes.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
Order primary succession on bare rock

lab.q: Challenge: what kind of species has a large effect on its ecosystem compared to its numbers? (two words)
lab.why: Removing a keystone species changes the whole system.

Challenge: succession starting on bare rock is called what? (two words, first word is the type)
lab.why: Succession on bare rock is primary succession.

learn.b: The birth rate and death rate are counted per 1000 people per year. The growth rate in percent is (births - deaths) / 10. If births are 20 and deaths are 10 per 1000, growth is 1 percent. Total fertility rate (TFR) is the average number of children per woman. Replacement level is about 2.1.

The rule of 70 estimates doubling time: 70 divided by the growth rate in percent. At 2 percent growth, a population doubles in 35 years. At 1 percent it takes 70 years. Growth that keeps adding a percent each year is called exponential.

Countries often move through four stages. Stage 1 has high birth and death rates. In stage 2 the death rate falls (better food and medicine), so the population grows fast. In stage 3 the birth rate falls. In stage 4 both are low. An age pyramid with a wide base shows many young people and fast growth.

qs.q: Using the rule of 70, how long does a population growing 2 percent per year take to double?
About what total fertility rate is replacement level?
qs.why: Slightly over 2 replaces both parents, allowing for early deaths.

qs.q: What does an age pyramid with a very wide base show?
o: Many young people and rapid growth
qs.why: A big young group means many future parents.

qs.q: What mainly causes the fast growth in stage 2 of the demographic transition?
o: Death rates fall while birth rates stay high
qs.why: Better food and medicine cut deaths first.

qs.q: A growth rate of 1 percent per year gives a doubling time of about 70 years.

Put the demographic transition stages in order

learn.b: Renewable energy sources are naturally replaced. Examples are solar, wind, hydroelectric, and geothermal energy. Geothermal uses heat from inside Earth.

Fossil fuels (coal, oil, and natural gas) take millions of years to form. Burning them releases carbon dioxide. Nuclear power uses uranium, a nonrenewable fuel, and releases almost no carbon dioxide while operating.
Most of Earth's fresh water is frozen in glaciers and ice sheets. Crop rotation helps keep nutrients in soil. Conservation means using resources wisely so they last.

qs.q: Which of these is a renewable energy source?
qs.why: Sunlight is constantly supplied.

qs.q: Which of these is a fossil fuel?
qs.why: Coal is a fossil fuel.

qs.q: Why do farmers practice crop rotation?
o: To help keep nutrients in the soil
qs.why: Different crops use and return different nutrients.

qs.q: Where is most of Earth's fresh water stored?
qs.why: Most fresh water is frozen.

qs.q: Nuclear power plants release large amounts of carbon dioxide while operating.
qs.why: They release almost none while operating.

Order how a coal power plant makes electricity

lab.why: Geothermal energy taps Earth's internal heat.

learn.b: Monoculture is growing one crop over a large area. It is efficient, but one pest or disease can wipe out a whole field. Tilling and bare soil cause erosion. Contour plowing, no-till farming, and crop rotation protect soil. Integrated pest management (IPM) mixes methods to control pests with fewer chemicals.

Urban sprawl spreads cities into farmland and wild habitat. Deforestation clears forests for farms and wood. Strip mining removes the surface layers to reach coal or minerals and can leave scars and pollution. Overgrazing can turn grassland into desert (desertification).

Worldwide, agriculture uses the most fresh water. An aquifer is an underground layer of water-bearing rock. If people pump water faster than it refills, the aquifer is depleted. Overfishing takes fish faster than they can reproduce.

qs.q: Which practice helps reduce soil erosion on a slope?
qs.why: Plowing across the slope slows water runoff.

qs.q: Which sector uses the most fresh water worldwide?
qs.why: Irrigation takes about 70 percent of withdrawals.

qs.q: What is a main risk of monoculture?
o: A single pest or disease can destroy the whole crop
qs.why: All plants are the same, so they share weaknesses.

qs.q: What is it called when water is pumped from an aquifer faster than it refills?
qs.why: The water table drops over time.

qs.q: Urban sprawl converts farmland and natural habitat into developed land.
qs.why: Cities spread outward and replace other land.

pairs: Mix of methods to control pests

qs.q: Put the soil layers in order from the surface down

lab.why: Crop rotation helps keep soil fertile.

lab.why: Integrated pest management combines several methods.

learn.b: Sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides from burning fossil fuels cause acid rain. Ground-level ozone is a main part of smog and harms lungs. Ozone high in the stratosphere is helpful because it blocks ultraviolet light.

A point source comes from one identifiable place, like a factory pipe. A nonpoint source is spread out, like runoff from farm fields. Fertilizer runoff causes eutrophication, which is overgrowth of algae.
Some toxins build up in organisms. Biomagnification means toxins become more concentrated at each higher level of the food chain.

qs.q: What mainly causes acid rain?
qs.why: These gases react with water in the air to make acids.

qs.q: What causes eutrophication in a lake?
qs.why: Nutrients cause algae blooms.

qs.q: Which is an example of nonpoint source pollution?
qs.why: Runoff comes from a wide area.

o: Toxins break down higher in the food chain
Toxins stay at the same level
Toxins become more concentrated up the food chain
qs.why: Top predators carry the highest toxin levels.

qs.q: A factory smokestack is an example of a nonpoint source of pollution.
qs.why: A smokestack is a single identifiable point source.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
pairs: Toxins build up up the food chain

qs.q: Order the steps of eutrophication

lab.why: Extra nutrients cause algae blooms and low oxygen.

lab.q: Challenge: farm runoff is a ___ source of pollution (point or nonpoint?)
lab.hint: It comes from a wide area.
lab.why: Runoff has no single pipe, so it is a nonpoint source.

lab.q: Challenge: which two oxides from burning fossil fuels cause acid rain? Name one.
lab.why: Sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides make acids in the air.

learn.b: Greenhouse gases like carbon dioxide, methane, and water vapor trap heat in the atmosphere. The natural greenhouse effect keeps Earth warm enough for life. Burning fossil fuels adds extra carbon dioxide.
A warming climate melts glaciers and ice sheets and warms the oceans, which raises sea level. It can also make heat waves and heavy storms more common.

Mitigation means reducing the causes, for example by switching to renewable energy, improving energy efficiency, and planting forests. Adaptation means adjusting to changes, such as building sea walls.

qs.q: Which of these is a greenhouse gas?
qs.why: Carbon dioxide traps heat.

qs.q: Which human activity adds the most carbon dioxide to the air?
qs.why: Coal, oil, and gas release stored carbon when burned.

qs.q: What helps raise sea level as the planet warms?
o: Melting land ice and warming oceans
qs.why: Water expands as it warms and ice melts into the sea.

qs.q: Which action most directly reduces greenhouse gas emissions?
qs.why: Renewables produce little carbon dioxide.

qs.q: The greenhouse effect is caused only by human activity.
qs.why: A natural greenhouse effect exists; humans have strengthened it.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
Order how the greenhouse effect works
items: Earth absorbs it and gives off heat

lab.q: Challenge: name a greenhouse gas other than carbon dioxide and water vapor.
lab.why: Methane and nitrous oxide are also greenhouse gases.

lab.q: Challenge: reducing the causes of climate change is called what?
Challenge: building sea walls is mitigation or adaptation?
lab.why: Sea walls help us live with rising seas.

learn.b: Most solid waste goes to landfills, which can leak pollutants. Incineration burns waste and makes energy, but can release air pollution. Composting turns food scraps and yard waste into fertilizer. The 3 Rs are reduce, reuse, recycle, and reducing is the best because it makes the least waste. E-waste and chemicals are hazardous waste.

In the US, the Clean Air Act and Clean Water Act limit pollution, and the Endangered Species Act protects at-risk species. The EPA enforces many environmental laws. The Montreal Protocol phased out ozone-damaging CFCs. The Paris Agreement aims to limit global warming.

Sustainability means meeting today's needs without harming future generations. Your ecological footprint is the land and water needed to support your lifestyle. The tragedy of the commons happens when people overuse a shared resource, like a fishery, because each gains by taking more.

qs.q: What did the Montreal Protocol target?
qs.why: CFCs were phased out to protect the ozone layer.

qs.q: Which of the 3 Rs is the best choice?
qs.why: Making less waste avoids the problem at its source.

qs.q: What is the tragedy of the commons?
o: A shared resource gets overused by individuals
qs.why: Each person benefits from taking more, but the resource is lost.

qs.q: What is compost?
o: Decomposed organic waste used as fertilizer
qs.why: Microbes break food and yard waste down into rich soil.

qs.q: The Paris Agreement aims to limit global warming.
qs.why: Countries pledged to cut emissions to limit warming.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning

qs.q: Put the waste choices in order from best to worst

lab.why: The Endangered Species Act protects at-risk species.

Challenge: which international treaty phased out CFCs? (two words)
lab.why: The Montreal Protocol protected the ozone layer.

learn.b: Water is polar, so its molecules form hydrogen bonds. This makes water cohesive and a good solvent. Proteins are built from amino acids, and nucleic acids are built from nucleotides.
Eukaryotic cells have a membrane-bound nucleus; prokaryotes do not. Mitochondria make ATP, ribosomes build proteins, and lysosomes break down waste. The cell membrane controls what enters and leaves.

Osmosis is the passive movement of water across a membrane. Active transport uses ATP to move substances against their gradient. A secreted protein travels from the rough ER to the Golgi to a vesicle.

qs.q: What type of bond holds water molecules together, giving water cohesion?
qs.why: Polar water molecules attract each other through hydrogen bonds.

qs.q: What is the monomer of a protein?
qs.why: Proteins are chains of amino acids.

qs.q: Which organelle produces most of a cell's ATP?
qs.why: Mitochondria carry out most cellular respiration.

qs.q: What is the passive movement of water across a membrane called?
qs.why: Osmosis needs no ATP; water moves toward higher solute concentration.

qs.q: Prokaryotic cells have a membrane-bound nucleus.
qs.why: Only eukaryotic cells have a membrane-bound nucleus.

Put the path of a secreted protein in order
items: Made on a ribosome at the rough ER

lab.q: Challenge: what type of bond holds water molecules to each other?
lab.hint: It forms between H and O of neighbors.
lab.why: Polar water molecules form hydrogen bonds.

lab.q: Challenge: what is the monomer of a protein? (two words)
lab.why: Proteins are chains of amino acids.

lab.q: Challenge: what is the property called when water molecules stick to each other?

learn.b: As a cell grows, its volume increases faster than its surface area, so the surface area to volume ratio (SA:V) falls. Small cells exchange materials more efficiently. Eukaryotes use organelles to compartmentalize reactions. Mitochondria and chloroplasts have their own circular DNA and ribosomes, which supports the endosymbiotic theory: they came from engulfed prokaryotes.

The membrane is a fluid mosaic of phospholipids and proteins. Passive transport needs no ATP. Simple diffusion moves small nonpolar molecules, and facilitated diffusion uses channel or carrier proteins. Active transport uses ATP to move a substance against its gradient. Endocytosis and exocytosis move large particles in vesicles.

Water potential (psi) predicts the direction of water movement: water moves from higher to lower water potential. Psi = psi_S + psi_P (solute plus pressure potential). Adding solute makes psi_S more negative. Pure water in an open container has psi = 0.

qs.q: As a cell gets larger, what happens to its surface area to volume ratio?
qs.why: Volume grows faster than surface area.

qs.q: Which observation best supports the endosymbiotic theory?
o: Mitochondria have their own circular DNA
qs.why: Prokaryote-like DNA suggests a bacterial origin.

qs.q: Facilitated diffusion moves molecules how?
o: Through channel or carrier proteins with no ATP
qs.why: It is passive but needs a protein pathway.

qs.q: Water moves toward which region?
qs.why: Water moves from high to low water potential.

qs.q: Active transport can move molecules from low concentration to high concentration.
qs.why: ATP energy pushes them against the gradient.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
Put the path of a secreted protein in order
items: Made on a ribosome at the rough ER

learn.b: Enzymes are proteins that speed up reactions by lowering the activation energy. They are not used up. Temperature and pH can change an enzyme's shape and its activity.
Photosynthesis happens in chloroplasts. The light reactions in the thylakoid membranes make ATP and NADPH, and the Calvin cycle in the stroma uses them to build glucose from carbon dioxide.

Cells break down glucose in four steps: glycolysis in the cytoplasm, pyruvate oxidation, the Krebs cycle, and the electron transport chain, which makes the most ATP. ATP is the cell's energy currency.

qs.q: What are the reactants of photosynthesis?
qs.why: Plants combine CO2 and H2O using light energy.

qs.q: Where do the light reactions occur in a chloroplast?
qs.why: Light-capturing pigments sit in the thylakoid membranes.

qs.q: Which stage of cellular respiration makes the most ATP?
qs.why: The electron transport chain drives ATP synthase.

qs.q: How do enzymes speed up reactions?
qs.why: Enzymes provide an easier path for the reaction.

qs.q: Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm and does not require oxygen.
qs.why: Glycolysis is the first, oxygen-independent step of respiration.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning

lab.why: Net gain from glycolysis is 2 ATP.

units.title: Cell Communication and the Cell Cycle

learn.b: Cell signaling has three steps. In reception, a ligand binds a receptor. In transduction, a relay such as a phosphorylation cascade or a second messenger like cAMP passes and amplifies the signal. In response, the cell changes gene expression or enzyme activity. Negative feedback keeps conditions stable. Positive feedback amplifies a change, as oxytocin does in childbirth.

The cell cycle has interphase (G1, S, G2) and the mitotic phase. DNA is replicated in S phase. Mitosis separates the chromosomes, then cytokinesis splits the cytoplasm. Checkpoints at G1, G2, and M make sure the cell is ready to continue.

Cyclins bind CDKs (cyclin-dependent kinases) to push the cell past checkpoints. The protein p53 stops the cycle or triggers apoptosis (programmed cell death) when DNA is damaged. Cancer is uncontrolled division, often from mutations in genes that control the cycle.

qs.q: What happens in the reception step of signaling?
o: A second messenger leaves the cell
qs.why: Reception is when the signal molecule binds.

qs.q: In which phase is DNA replicated?
qs.why: S stands for synthesis of DNA.

qs.q: Which proteins work together to drive the cell cycle forward?
qs.why: Cyclin-CDK complexes trigger checkpoints.

qs.q: Which is an example of positive feedback?
o: A thermostat turning off a heater
qs.why: Each contraction triggers more oxytocin, amplifying the change.

qs.q: Negative feedback tends to amplify a change.

learn.b: Mitosis makes two genetically identical cells. Meiosis makes gametes with half the number of chromosomes, and crossing over and independent assortment create variety.
An allele is a version of a gene. Genotype is the genetic makeup and phenotype is the observable trait. A cross of Aa x Aa gives a 3:1 phenotype ratio when one allele is completely dominant.
In DNA, A pairs with T and C pairs with G. Transcription copies DNA into mRNA. In translation, a ribosome reads mRNA codons (three bases) and tRNA brings the matching amino acids.

learn.b: Helicase unwinds the double helix and primase lays down an RNA primer. DNA polymerase adds nucleotides only in the 5' to 3' direction. The leading strand is made continuously. The lagging strand is made in short Okazaki fragments, which DNA ligase joins.

RNA polymerase binds a promoter and transcribes DNA into mRNA. In eukaryotes the pre-mRNA gets a 5' cap and a poly-A tail, and introns are spliced out, leaving exons. In translation, the start codon is AUG, tRNA anticodons match codons, and stop codons (UAA, UAG, UGA) end the chain.

In the lac operon, the repressor blocks transcription until lactose binds it, so the genes turn on only when lactose is present. Eukaryotes also use transcription factors. Tools include PCR to copy DNA, gel electrophoresis to separate fragments by size, and CRISPR to edit genes.

learn.b: Individuals vary, and some traits help them survive and reproduce more. Over generations, those traits become more common in the population. Mutations are the original source of new alleles.
Darwin and Wallace proposed natural selection. Speciation is the formation of new species, often after populations become isolated. A niche is an organism's role in its ecosystem.

Producers make their own food. Energy flows from producers to consumers, and only about 10% of energy passes to the next trophic level. A population is one species in an area; a community includes all species there.

learn.b: Exponential growth follows dN/dt = rN and happens when resources are unlimited. Logistic growth follows dN/dt = rN(K - N)/K and levels off at the carrying capacity K. Density-dependent factors, like competition and disease, matter more as a population gets crowded. Density-independent factors, like storms and fires, do not depend on crowding.

Species interact. In mutualism both benefit, in commensalism one benefits and the other is unaffected, and in parasitism one benefits and the other is harmed. Competition happens when species use the same limited resource. A keystone species affects the community far more than its numbers suggest. Succession is the change in a community over time.

Net primary productivity is the energy left after producers' respiration (GPP minus respiration). About 10 percent of energy passes to the next trophic level. Ecosystems are disrupted by invasive species, habitat loss, pollution, and climate change, which can lower biodiversity.

qs.q: In logistic growth, what happens as the population nears K?
qs.why: The (K - N)/K term shrinks, slowing growth.

qs.why: Competition gets stronger as density rises.

learn.b: The atomic number is the number of protons. Isotopes have the same protons but different neutrons. Valence electrons are the outer electrons that take part in bonding.

Moving left to right across a period, ionization energy and electronegativity generally increase. Fluorine has the highest electronegativity. Electrons fill subshells in order: 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, and so on.
Ionic bonds form between a metal and a nonmetal when electrons transfer. Covalent bonds form between nonmetals when electrons are shared. A cation is a positive ion.

qs.why: Atomic number equals the number of protons.

qs.why: Greater nuclear charge holds electrons more tightly.

learn.b: London dispersion forces exist in all particles and grow with more electrons. Dipole-dipole forces act between polar molecules. A hydrogen bond is a strong dipole-dipole force when H is bonded to N, O, or F. Ion-dipole forces hold ions in water. Stronger forces mean a higher boiling point and lower vapor pressure.

The ideal gas law is PV = nRT, with R = 0.0821 L atm/(mol K) and T in kelvins. At STP, 1 mol of gas takes up 22.4 L. Boyle's law: P1V1 = P2V2 at constant T and n. Dalton's law: the total pressure is the sum of the partial pressures. Kinetic molecular theory says temperature is proportional to average kinetic energy.

Molarity is moles of solute per liter of solution. Spectroscopy uses light to study substances. In Beer's law, A = (epsilon)(b)(c): absorbance is proportional to concentration, so a darker solution absorbs more light. Chromatography separates a mixture based on how strongly each part sticks to the stationary phase.

learn.b: An exothermic reaction releases heat and has a negative change in enthalpy (delta H). An endothermic reaction absorbs heat. Heat transfer is calculated with q = mc(delta T).

Rates depend on concentration, temperature, and catalysts. Higher temperature means more collisions with enough energy, so the rate usually goes up. Activation energy is the energy needed to start a reaction.
A catalyst lowers the activation energy and is not used up. Entropy measures disorder, and nature tends toward more disorder.

learn.b: A rate law has the form rate = k[A]^m[B]^n. The orders m and n must be found by experiment, not from the coefficients. If doubling [A] doubles the rate, the order is 1. If it quadruples the rate, the order is 2. If it has no effect, the order is 0. The units of k depend on the overall order; for first order, k is in s^-1.
Zero order: [A] vs time is a straight line. First order: ln[A] vs time is a straight line, and the half-life is t1/2 = 0.693 / k, which stays constant. Second order: 1/[A] vs time is a straight line.

A mechanism is a series of elementary steps. The slowest step is the rate-determining step. An intermediate is made and then used up, while a catalyst is used and then regenerated. Collision theory and the Arrhenius idea say that more molecules have enough activation energy as temperature rises.

Enthalpy change is a state function, so you can add the delta H values of steps. If you reverse a reaction, change the sign of delta H. If you multiply a reaction, multiply delta H by the same factor. The standard enthalpy of formation of an element in its standard state is zero.

delta H(rxn) = sum of delta Hf of products - sum of delta Hf of reactants. With bond energies, delta H = energy of bonds broken - energy of bonds formed. Breaking bonds takes energy (endothermic) and forming bonds releases it (exothermic).

learn.b: At equilibrium, the forward and reverse reaction rates are equal, so concentrations stay constant. The equilibrium constant K is the ratio of products to reactants. Le Chatelier's principle says a system shifts to oppose a change.
An acid donates H+ and a base accepts H+. A strong acid like HCl fully ionizes in water, while a weak acid like acetic acid does not.
pH measures acidity. At 25 C, pH 7 is neutral, below 7 is acidic, and above 7 is basic. A buffer resists changes in pH.

learn.b: pH = -log[H+] and pOH = -log[OH-]. At 25 C, pH + pOH = 14 and Kw = 1.0 x 10^-14. A strong acid like HCl ionizes completely, so 0.01 M HCl has pH 2. A weak acid ionizes only a little and is described by Ka. A larger Ka means a stronger acid.

A buffer holds a nearly constant pH. It contains a weak acid and its conjugate base. Added acid reacts with the base, and added base reacts with the acid. The Henderson-Hasselbalch equation is pH = pKa + log([A-]/[HA]). When [A-] = [HA], pH = pKa.

In a titration, a solution of known concentration is added to an unknown one. At the equivalence point, moles of acid equal moles of base. For a strong acid with a strong base, the equivalence point is at pH 7. For a weak acid, the pH at the half-equivalence point equals pKa.

learn.b: Entropy (S) measures how spread out energy and matter are. Gases have more entropy than liquids, and liquids more than solids. Delta G = delta H - T(delta S). A reaction is spontaneous if delta G is negative. If delta H is negative and delta S is positive, it is spontaneous at all temperatures. Delta G is related to K by delta G = -RT ln K, so K > 1 means a negative delta G.

A galvanic cell uses a spontaneous redox reaction to make electricity. Oxidation happens at the anode and reduction at the cathode. Electrons flow from anode to cathode. E(cell) = E(cathode) - E(anode), and a positive E(cell) means the reaction is spontaneous. Also, delta G = -nFE.
An electrolytic cell uses electricity to force a nonspontaneous reaction. Charge is q = It. Moles of electrons = q / F, where F = 96,485 C/mol. More current or more time plates out more metal.

qs.q: When delta H is negative and delta S is positive, what is true?

qs.why: Delta G = delta H - T delta S is always negative.

qs.why: Gas particles are the most spread out.
